fixes.answer: It really depends on the person and the job. Working from home offers wonderful flexibility and eliminates the commute, which many find [[liberating]] and more productive. However, the office provides valuable social interaction, easier collaboration and a clearer boundary between work and home life. Personally, I think a [[hybrid]] model captures the best of both, though it requires real [[self-discipline]] to work remotely well.

Automation is a genuine [[double-edged sword]]. On one hand, it will [[inevitably]] [[displace]] many workers in routine and manual jobs, which is a serious concern. On the other hand, history shows that technology also creates entirely new industries and roles. The key effect is a shift in the types of jobs available, which means workforces will need to adapt and acquire new skills.
fixes.why: 'shift' and 'adapt' are plain; marked 'double-edged sword' and 'inevitably'

fixes.answer: The societal impact could be substantial. If automation [[concentrates wealth]], it may [[widen inequality]], which is a real danger. The rise of the gig economy also brings flexibility but often [[at the cost of]] job security and benefits. On a positive note, more flexible work could improve work-life balance. Managing these changes fairly will be one of the great challenges of our era, requiring thoughtful policy.
fixes.why: 'challenges' and 'policy' are plain; marked 'concentrates wealth', 'widen inequality', 'at the cost of'

fixes.answer: I think it is a real possibility, and one I would welcome. As automation boosts productivity, there is a strong argument that the gains could be shared through shorter working weeks. Trials of the four-day week seem to have shown [[promising]] results, with productivity maintained. However, this will not happen automatically; it will require [[deliberate choices]] by businesses and governments to [[prioritise]] wellbeing over pure output.
fixes.why: 'maintained' is plain; marked 'deliberate choices'; softened the claim about trials

fixes.answer: The single most important thing is to embrace lifelong learning. Workers should continually update their skills and remain [[adaptable]], rather than assuming their current expertise will last forever. Developing [[transferable skills]], like communication and problem-solving, is wise, since these remain valuable across industries. Staying curious and open to change is really the best [[safeguard]] against being left behind.

The gig economy offers genuine advantages: flexibility, independence and the ability to work for multiple clients, which suits many people. However, the disadvantages are considerable, [[chiefly]] the lack of job security, steady income and benefits like sick pay or pensions. This [[precariousness]] can be very stressful. So while it offers freedom, it often shifts significant risk onto the individual worker, which needs better [[regulation]].
